name: Myths from Mesopotamia: Creation, the Flood, Gilgamesh, and Others, translated with an introduction and notes by Stephanie Dalley (Oxford University Press)
date: 1989 (Oxford University Press hardback). Paperback in the World's Classics / Oxford World's Classics series from 1991 [uncertain: exact year]; revised edition 2000, which took account of newly published tablets and advances in grammar and lexicography; current Oxford World's Classics reissue ISBN 9780199538362 (2008) [uncertain: reissue year]
creator: Stephanie Dalley, Assyriologist at the Oriental Institute, University of Oxford (taught Akkadian and Sumerian there 1979 to 2007; Shillito Fellow in Assyriology from 1988; later Honorary Senior Fellow, Somerville College). Published by Oxford University Press
form: Scholarly anthology of verse-lineated literal translations. Gilgamesh sits beside Atrahasis, the Descent of Ishtar, Nergal and Ereshkigal, Adapa, Etana, the Epic of Creation (Enuma Elish), the Theogony of Dunnu, Anzu and Erra and Ishum, each with its own introduction, notes and a shared glossary of names
translator_access: Direct access. Dalley is a cuneiformist who read and taught Akkadian and Sumerian at Oxford, and she translated from the cuneiform sources and their editions, not from a crib. The 2000 revision updated the text in light of new tablets and philological work (OUP catalogue description)
scholarly_adviser: N/A in the Armitage/Mitchell sense: Dalley is herself the specialist, so there is no named scholar behind a poet's version
versions_used: Two separate translations in one book: the Standard Babylonian eleven-tablet epic (plus Tablet XII), and after it the Old Babylonian version given on its own terms from the surviving early tablets (including the Pennsylvania and Yale tablets and the Sippar/Meissner tablet with Siduri's advice) [uncertain: full list of OB witnesses]. The book as a whole places Gilgamesh in its Akkadian mythological setting, so the flood story can be read against Atrahasis and Ishtar against the Descent of Ishtar. Predates George's critical edition (2003) and the Sulaymaniyah tablet (published 2014), so neither is present
non_standard_material: Kept apart rather than merged. Instead of patching Standard Babylonian gaps with Old Babylonian lines inside one continuous narrative, Dalley prints the Old Babylonian version as a distinct text after the Standard one. The reader who wants Siduri's 'let your stomach be full' speech finds it in the Old Babylonian section, not stitched into Tablet X [uncertain: whether any OB lines are also imported into the SB text in the revised edition]
gap_policy: Shown, not bridged. Breaks in the tablets are left as breaks, with line numbers and editorial notes indicating how much is lost; Dalley does not invent connective narrative. Notes and the per-text introductions explain what is missing and why [uncertain: exact form of gap notes]
typography_of_absence: Scholarly apparatus on the page: ellipses for broken words and lines, square brackets for restored text, parentheses for words supplied for sense, and indications of gaps of a given number of lines between columns [uncertain: exact conventions]. Because the Standard and Old Babylonian texts are printed separately, the page shows two incomplete witnesses rather than one smoothed story
tablet_xii: Included as part of the Standard Babylonian translation, with Dalley's introduction treating it as an appended Akkadian rendering of the Sumerian 'Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Netherworld' rather than an organic continuation [uncertain]. Including it means the Standard text closes on Enkidu's grim report from the Netherworld, not on the walls of Uruk, though the reader is told why
turning_point: The death of Enkidu drives the second half, but Dalley's two-text structure gives the reader two hinges. In the Standard Babylonian version the decisive moment is Tablet XI: Ut-napishtim's flood story, the failed test of staying awake six days and seven nights, and the snake taking the plant ('A snake smelt the fragrance of the plant. It came up silently and carried off the plant. As it took it away, it shed its scaly skin'). In the Old Babylonian version the hinge is Siduri, whose advice ('You will not find the eternal life you seek') states the lesson outright. Printing Atrahasis in the same book also shifts weight onto the flood episode, which reads as a borrowed piece of a wider mythology
arc_interpretation: Acceptance of mortality set within a shared Mesopotamian cosmology, rather than a self-contained heroic arc. Because the anthology sets Gilgamesh beside the creation and flood myths, the story reads as one instance of a recurring theme: the gods keep life for themselves ('When the gods created mankind / They appointed death for mankind, / Kept eternal life in their own hands', Old Babylonian Siduri). Dalley's literal restraint leaves interpretation to the reader; her introductions stress textual history and parallels over moral reading
key_passages: Shamhat and Enkidu (Tablet I): 'Shamhat did for him, the primitive man, as women do. His love-making he lavished upon her', after which Enkidu has lost his animal speed and gained understanding. Plain and brisk, with 'primitive man' for lullu. Siduri (Old Babylonian version): 'Gilgamesh, where do you roam? You will not find the eternal life you seek. When the gods created mankind / They appointed death for mankind, / Kept eternal life in their own hands.' She then urges him to 'let your stomach be full, / Day and night enjoy yourself in every way', to dance and play and cherish wife and child. Snake (Tablet XI): 'A snake smelt the fragrance of the plant. / It came up silently and carried off the plant. / As it took it away, it shed its scaly skin.' Death in the bedchamber and the closing walls of Uruk (Tablet XI) are rendered in the same literal register [uncertain: exact wording not verified]
diction_and_metre: No metre. Literal British English in short lines matching the Akkadian line units, with modest archaic colour in phrasing ('Of him who found out all things, I shall tell the land') and Mesopotamian epithets kept ('Uruk the Sheepfold'). Proper names are hyphenated to show their parts (Ut-napishtim, Ur-shanabi). Reads as a careful scholar's working text, clearer than a transliteration but not shaped as poetry
sample_line: "Of him who found out all things, I shall tell the land, / Of him who experienced everything, I shall teach the whole." (Tablet I, opening; Dalley, Myths from Mesopotamia, OUP 1989, p. 50)
critical_response: Widely respected and heavily used in university teaching. The Comparative Civilizations Review judged that 'Dalley obviously controls the material as a scholar', and the book is credited with making the Babylonian corpus accessible for the first time to general students of mythology (quoted in OUP and retailer descriptions). Oxford University Press uses its Gilgamesh as a teaching excerpt in the Patterns of World History resources. For Gilgamesh specifically it has been overtaken for scholarly purposes by Andrew George's Penguin translation (1999) and critical edition (2003), but it remains a standard reference for the wider Akkadian myths [uncertain: specific journal reviews of the 1989 edition]
controversies: None over the Gilgamesh translation's accuracy or liberties. Dalley is better known for an unrelated dispute: her argument (developed over eighteen years and set out in her 2013 book) that the Hanging Gardens were at Nineveh under Sennacherib rather than at Babylon. The book is also cited heavily on ancient-astronaut websites, a misuse outside her control
regional_reception: English-language academic edition published in Oxford; no known Arabic or Kurdish translation of this volume and no recorded return to Iraq as a book [uncertain]. Its reach is global through the Oxford World's Classics series, and an audiobook edition has since appeared
ai_craft_tension: Dalley's book shows the human work that sits around a translation rather than inside a line. A machine can now produce a literal Akkadian-to-English rendering close to her register, and her 2000 revision already shows the text updating as new tablets arrived, which is the part automated fragment matching could speed up. What a machine does not yet do is the editorial framing: deciding to print the Old Babylonian and Standard versions as two texts instead of one blended story, and deciding to put Gilgamesh next to Atrahasis and the Descent of Ishtar so a reader sees the flood and the goddess as shared myth. That curatorial choice changes how the arc reads more than any single word choice does
essay_hooks: (1) The famous carpe diem speech from Siduri is not in the Standard version at all; in Dalley it sits in a separate Old Babylonian section, so the book's most quoted advice comes from a different, older text. (2) Gilgamesh is one myth among ten in the volume, placed next to Atrahasis, whose flood the epic borrows. (3) The opening, 'Of him who found out all things, I shall tell the land', is a claim about knowledge, not strength. (4) The snake 'came up silently and carried off the plant. As it took it away, it shed its scaly skin': the whole quest undone in three lines. (5) The translator is better known in the press for relocating the Hanging Gardens to Nineveh, a reminder that the same philology that reads Gilgamesh also rewrites wonders of the world. Sources: OUP Learning Link excerpt of Dalley 1989; OUP catalogue page; Wikipedia 'Stephanie Dalley'
